intro: In the last unit, prices moved freely. When lemonade got popular, its price rose; when concert tickets were scarce, resale prices jumped. This unit asks what happens when a price is not allowed to move, and what happens when a price moves freely but still leaves something out. A gas station in 1973 with a line around the block, an apartment with forty applicants, a river that turned brown below a paper mill, and a fireworks show nobody would pay for are all part of the same story.

The first chapter looks at price ceilings and price floors: rent control, the minimum wage, farm price supports and the gasoline lines of the 1970s. You will see why a ceiling below the market price creates a shortage, why a floor above it creates a surplus, and what takes the place of price when price cannot ration: lines, lotteries, favoritism and black markets. You will also see who really pays a tax. The second chapter looks at market failure: pollution and other externalities, public goods and free riders, overused common resources, and deals where one side knows more than the other.

By the end, you will be able to take a real policy, such as a cap on rents, a tax on pollution or a subsidy for flu shots, and predict what it does with numbers. You will be able to say who gains, who loses and what the policy costs. Economists do not all agree on these questions, and neither will your classmates. The goal is not one right opinion. The goal is to argue from the model and the numbers, and to name the trade-offs honestly.
bigQuestion: When should government step into a market, by setting prices, taxing, regulating or providing goods itself, and how can we tell if it made things better or worse?

timeline.t: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations names public works that no private person would build as a duty of government
Arthur Pigou's The Economics of Welfare argues for taxing costs that spill onto others
The Agricultural Adjustment Act begins federal programs to hold up farm prices
The Fair Labor Standards Act sets the first federal minimum wage, 25 cents an hour
Wartime ration books and price controls cover sugar, meat, gasoline and tires
Paul Samuelson gives the modern definition of a public good
Ronald Coase shows how clear property rights and bargaining can settle some spillover costs
Garrett Hardin names the tragedy of the commons
The EPA is created, and George Akerlof publishes his paper on lemons and hidden quality
An oil embargo and price controls on gasoline bring long lines at the pump
Federal price controls on oil and gasoline end, and the lines do not return
The Clean Air Act Amendments create a cap-and-trade market to cut sulfur dioxide

words.d: a legal maximum price; it creates a shortage only when it is set below the equilibrium price
a legal minimum price; it creates a surplus only when it is set above the equilibrium price
a price control is binding when it actually changes the market price: a ceiling below equilibrium or a floor above it
the amount by which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a price held below equilibrium
the amount by which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a price held above equilibrium
buying and selling at prices or in ways the law forbids, which grows wherever a price control binds
who actually bears a tax after prices adjust; the less elastic side of the market bears more
a cost or benefit of a deal that falls on people who were not part of it, such as pollution or the protection from a vaccine
the full cost of producing something: the producer's private cost plus the external cost to others
a good that is non-rival and non-excludable, such as national defense, which markets tend not to provide
someone who enjoys a good without paying for it because nobody can keep them from using it
the overuse of a resource that everyone may use and nobody owns, because each user ignores the cost to others

test.q: A city caps downtown parking at $2 an hour where the market rate would be $5. What is the most likely result?
choices: No change, because the cap is non-binding
Drivers circle for a long time looking for spaces that are almost always full
test.why: A ceiling below equilibrium binds and creates a shortage. Time spent circling takes over the rationing job the price cannot do.

test.q: At a $6 price floor, sellers offer 500 units and buyers want 350. What does the floor create?
test.why: Surplus = quantity supplied minus quantity demanded = 500 - 350 = 150 units.

test.q: When the price of lumber rises, sawmills add a second shift because they can now earn more. Which job of a price is this?
test.why: A higher price rewards producers for making more. That is the motivate job.

test.q: A 50-cent tax per pack of batteries is collected from sellers. The price buyers pay rises from $5.00 to $5.10. Who bears more of the tax?
test.why: Buyers pay $0.10 more. Sellers keep $5.10 - $0.50 = $4.60, which is $0.40 less than before, so sellers bear more.

test.q: Which statement best describes what economists say about the minimum wage?
choices: All agree a moderate increase destroys many jobs
All agree it has no effect on jobs
The simple model predicts fewer jobs, and economists disagree about how large the effect is for moderate increases
All agree it lowers the pay of workers who keep their jobs
test.why: The price-floor model predicts a surplus of labor. Studies of moderate increases give mixed results, so the size of the effect is debated.

test.q: Over ten years, what usually happens to the housing shortage under a binding rent control?
choices: It disappears as renters leave the city
It grows, because fewer rental units are built and existing ones are kept up less
It stays the same, because housing supply never changes
test.why: Housing supply is inelastic in the short run but responds over time. A capped rent discourages building and upkeep, so supply shrinks.

test.q: A concert venue's private cost is $20 per ticket sold, and the noise imposes $5 of harm per ticket on neighbors. What is the social cost per ticket?
test.why: Social cost = private cost + external cost = $20 + $5 = $25.

test.q: Which of these is closest to a pure public good?
choices: A flood-control levee that protects a whole town
test.why: A levee protects everyone behind it at once (non-rival), and no one in town can be left unprotected (non-excludable).

test.q: Why do many governments subsidize flu shots?
choices: Flu shots have a negative externality
Flu shots cannot be sold in a market
Buyers leave out the protection their shot gives to others, so the market provides too few
test.why: A positive externality means social benefit is above private benefit. A subsidy lowers the price so more people get the shot.

test.q: In a cap-and-trade system, what does the government fix?
choices: The total amount of pollution allowed
The cleanup cost at each plant
The number of firms in the industry
test.why: The cap sets the total number of permits, so total pollution is fixed. The permit price is left to the market.

test.q: Why do open-access fisheries tend to be overfished?
choices: Each fisher ignores how his catch reduces what is left for everyone else
Fish prices are held down by law
test.why: In a commons, each user bears only his own costs, not the cost his use imposes on others. That leads to overuse.

test.q: An insurer prices a plan for the average person. Mostly people who expect big medical bills sign up, and healthy people skip it. What is this called?
test.why: When buyers know more about their own risk than the seller does, the people who show up to buy are the most costly ones.

test.q: A city caps concert tickets at $40, and on show night tickets resell outside for $150. What caused the resale market?
choices: A price floor that created a surplus
A binding price ceiling that created a shortage
A fall in demand for the concert
test.why: The cap held the price below equilibrium. Fans who could not buy at $40 bid up the tickets that leaked out.

test.q: A small group of producers spends millions lobbying to keep a program that raises their prices and costs each consumer a few dollars a year. What is this called?
test.why: Rent-seeking is spending effort to win favors from government instead of producing. Concentrated gains organize; scattered losses do not.

test.q: Under a price ceiling on gasoline, a driver waits 3 hours to save $6. What did her waiting earn per hour?
test.why: $6 saved ÷ 3 hours = $2 an hour. Rationing by waiting costs time that no seller receives.

write.prompt: Your city council proposes capping one-bedroom rents at $1,200 a month where the market rent is $1,600. Make up a small supply-and-demand table, predict the shortage now and in ten years, compare rent control with one other tool such as a housing voucher or allowing more building, and argue which you would choose.
tips: Say whether the cap is binding and show the shortage with numbers from your table.
Explain why supply changes little in year one but more over ten years.
Name who gains and who loses: tenants with leases, newcomers, landlords, taxpayers.
Describe how apartments get rationed if price cannot do it: waiting lists, key fees, favoritism.
Give the strongest argument for the side you did not choose, then say why yours wins.
